opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've spent a good chunk of my career working from Singapore while a lot of the center of gravity in AI has been in the Bay Area. Honestly, I think geography matters less than people assume for the actual *work*, and more than people admit for the *culture* around it.

On the work side, research these days is really about compute access, good infrastructure, and a tight feedback loop with your collaborators. If you have those, you can do frontier work from anywhere. A lot of the stuff I'm proudest of was done with people I'd barely met in person. You're on chat, you're reading each other's code, you're looking at the same loss curves. The model doesn't care what time zone you're in.

But there's a cost. Time zones are real. If your collaborators are twelve or fifteen hours away, you lose that rapid back-and-forth where someone says "hey, try this" and twenty minutes later you have an answer. You end up working odd hours, taking late-night calls, and you have to be very deliberate about writing things down clearly so people can pick up your work while you sleep. Funnily enough, that sometimes becomes an advantage. It's almost like a relay race, things keep moving around the clock.

The bigger thing, I think, is the informal stuff. In the Bay Area, so much happens over coffee, at dinners, at random meetups. You hear about what's working and what's not before it ever shows up on arXiv. That ambient information flow is hard to replicate remotely. So if you're outside the hub, you have to compensate by being more intentional: reading a lot, being active online, traveling when it counts, building relationships proactively.

And I'd also say there's real talent everywhere. Some of the strongest researchers I've worked with came from places that aren't traditionally seen as AI hubs. Being distributed lets you tap into that. So my overall take is: geography is a friction, not a wall. If you're good and you're plugged in, you can do great work from anywhere, but you have to work a bit harder to stay in the loop.

r001.rationale: The response discusses geography, hubs, and distributed talent, but does not question whether countries are meaningful units for understanding AI research.

r002.rationale: It describes collaboration across time zones as a relay race where work keeps moving around the clock.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, honestly, because I'm based in Singapore and almost everyone I work with is somewhere else. It's a weird setup. I spent years at Google working out of Singapore while most of the team was in Mountain View, and then with Reka it was the same thing, people in the Bay Area, London, me in Singapore.

I think the honest answer is that geography matters way less than people assume for the actual research, and way more than people assume for the career and the social side of it.

For the research itself, like, I've written a lot of papers with people I've never met in person. The work happens in docs and Slack and in the training runs. You look at the loss curves together, you argue about the ablations, that's fine remotely. If anything, being on the opposite side of the world is kind of a hack, because I wake up and there's a whole day of results waiting for me, and then I hand things off when I go to sleep. There's a sort of follow-the-sun thing that happens naturally.

But the thing that's hard is the serendipity. So much of what happens in AI right now happens in conversations in the Bay Area that you don't even know occurred. Someone mentions an idea at a dinner, someone else picks it up, and three months later there's a trend and you're like, where did this come from? When you're remote, you're always slightly downstream of that. You're reading about things rather than being in the room when they're decided. I felt that a lot at Google, where decisions about what directions were hot got made in hallway conversations I wasn't in. You just have to be more intentional, you have to travel more, you have to be louder online, basically. I think my Twitter presence partly exists because of this, right? It's how I stay in the conversation without physically being there.

The other thing is time zones are genuinely brutal for anything that's not async. I've taken a lot of 2 a.m. meetings. And there's a real cost to that over years. It's not free.

So I guess my take is, if you're a strong researcher you can do the work from anywhere, and I'd actually encourage people not to feel like they need to be in SF to contribute. But you have to be realistic that you're going to pay a tax on visibility and on being early to things, and you need to actively compensate for it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses geography’s effect on research and careers, but does not question whether countries are meaningful units for understanding AI research.

r002.rationale: It describes waking to a day of results and handing work off at bedtime as a natural “follow-the-sun” workflow across time zones.

astra-6.text:
I think geography still matters, even though you can collaborate with people anywhere. There’s a difference between having a scheduled call and being in the same room, where you can throw out an idea, get a reaction, and keep going. Time zones also affect how quickly you can iterate. A small question can turn into a whole day of waiting.

But I don’t think that means good research has to happen in one place. For a distributed team, you need to be more deliberate about communication—write things down, make it easy for people to pick up where you left off, and have enough overlap to discuss the difficult bits. The important thing is building a group where people trust each other and can exchange ideas freely. Being nearby helps with that, but it isn’t the only way to get there.

r001.rationale: It discusses proximity and distributed collaboration, but does not question whether countries are meaningful units for understanding AI research.

r002.rationale: It says time zones can delay iteration; it does not identify round-the-clock coverage as a reason to distribute collaborators.

sol-6.1.text:
I think geography still matters, even when the collaboration is international. You can work on a paper with someone anywhere, but being in the same room makes it easier to build trust, exchange half-formed ideas, and figure out what to work on next. Those interactions are harder to schedule over a call.

At the same time, I don’t think good research belongs to a particular place. What matters is having people you can learn from, access to the resources you need, and the freedom to pursue an idea. With collaborators across time zones, you have to be more deliberate about writing things down and making time to talk. So geography shapes how collaboration happens, but it doesn’t have to define its limits.
